Stocks rally as Treasury yields fall; S&P 500 closes at a record

Published 2026-10-07 15:15 UTC

Stocks climbed on Tuesday as Treasury yields fell, lifting the S&P 500 to a record close. The benchmark index gained 1.1%, the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added about 380 points. Technology and real estate stocks led the advance, while energy shares lagged.

The 10-year Treasury yield dropped to 3.9% from 4.05% a day earlier after a weaker-than-expected reading on job openings. Lower yields make stocks more attractive relative to bonds and reduce borrowing costs for companies, and investors bid up shares of fast-growing technology firms that are most sensitive to interest rates.

Homebuilders were among the biggest gainers as mortgage rates followed bond yields lower. Several home construction stocks rose more than 4%. Utilities, which often trade like bonds because of their steady dividends, also rose. Bank stocks were mixed: lower long-term rates can squeeze lending margins, but investors also expect loan demand to pick up.

Strategists cautioned that the rally rests on expectations of further easing in borrowing costs, and that a hot inflation report next week could reverse the move. Trading volume was slightly below average, suggesting some investors were waiting for more data before committing new money.

Small-cap stocks outperformed, with the Russell 2000 gaining 1.8%. Smaller companies tend to carry more floating-rate debt, so they benefit more directly when yields fall. The index remains below its peak from three years ago, and some analysts see room for it to catch up with large caps if the economy avoids a sharp slowdown.

In commodities, gold rose 0.6% as the dollar weakened, while crude futures slipped. Bitcoin gained 2%. The CBOE Volatility Index, a gauge of expected swings in the stock market, fell to its lowest level since August, indicating that options traders are not bracing for a sudden selloff in the coming weeks.
